passage: Gopika, since you keep telling me you don't want to be pushy, let old Ujjwal tell you about my rule. When I was twenty-one I wrote to an engineer and heard nothing. I did not know whether to write again or drop it. I stayed awake over it. Then a senior said, "Make a rule beforehand, so your head doesn't argue." Mine was: if there is no answer in a week, I send one short, polite follow-up. After that, I let it go and think no worse of anyone. A week passed. I sent two lines: "Just checking that my message did not get buried. No worries if the timing is bad." No reply. I closed the tab and felt calm. Three months later that same engineer nodded to me at a conference and said, "Sorry, I missed it. Ask me now."

qa.q: How long did Ujjwal's rule say to wait before following up?
qa.a: Ujjwal's rule said to wait a week.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling before the rule was made?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt unsettled and stuck, unsure whether to write again and lying awake over it.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept Ujjwal calm after no reply, and why?
qa.a: Ujjwal made the rule beforehand and closed the tab once it was used, because the decision was already made and there was nothing left to argue with oneself about.

qa.q: How might the engineer have seen the follow-up?
qa.a: The engineer received a short, polite note with no pressure, which may explain the friendly remark at the conference months later.

grounding: Shows an if-then plan for following up once after a week and then moving on without resentment.
